name: objdump
plain: `objdump` shows what is inside a compiled program or object file, and above all it can disassemble it: turn the machine code back into assembly instructions you can read.
Use it to find the function that checks a password, to see which strings and constants are stored, and to check headers and symbols without running the file.
when: Read the assembly of main or of a suspicious function.
Dump a data section such as .rodata.
Check headers, symbols and relocations without a full disassembler.

examples.title: Mix source and assembly  (-S)
examples.cmd: gcc -g -o hello_g hello.c && objdump -S -M intel --no-show-raw-insn hello_g | sed -n '/<main>:/,/ret/p' | head -16

mistakes: Forgetting -M intel: AT&T syntax puts the source before the destination, the opposite of most books.
Disassembling a stripped binary and finding no function names: use --start-address or a tool like Ghidra.
Reading data as code with -D: it prints nonsense instructions.
Expecting objdump to follow what the program does at run time: it is static.
try: Find the strcmp call in main and the jump after it.
Compile hello.c with and without -O2 and compare the assembly of main.
Dump .rodata with -s -j and match the strings with strings -t x.
Patch plan: find the file offset of a jump with -F, then edit it with xxd.
see_also: readelf(1), nm(1), gdb(1), Ghidra, radare2 and rizin, strings(1), xxd(1).
